facts.raw_span: a 76-year-old woman
history of appendicitis, torsion of an ovarian cyst pedicle, and uterine myoma
rapidly enlarging right parietal mass behind the ear over one month
no neurological deficits or systemic symptoms
laboratory studies, including complete blood counts, metabolic panel, and viral serology for HIV and Epstein-Barr virus, were all normal or negative
Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a 5-cm hyperdense meningeal mass with parietal bone invasion
Gadolinium-enhanced MRI showed a heterogeneously enhancing lesion in the right parietal region
Cerebral angiography demonstrated a vascular tumor supplied by the middle meningeal artery
a clinical diagnosis of osteoblastic meningioma was made
intraoperatively, the tumor was extradural, caused skull destruction, and had no intradural involvement
Histology showed a malignant spindle cell neoplasm
positive immunostaining for α-smooth muscle actin, vimentin, and desmin, and negative staining for Epstein-Barr virus

concepts.why: The patient presented with a rapidly enlarging right parietal mass, and imaging studies revealed a hyperdense meningeal mass with parietal bone invasion, consistent with a meningioma.
The clinical diagnosis of osteoblastic meningioma was made based on the patient's presentation and imaging findings.
Histology showed a malignant spindle cell neoplasm with positive immunostaining for α-smooth muscle actin, vimentin, and desmin, consistent with a spindle cell neoplasm.
The patient's presentation and imaging findings are consistent with a primary lymphoma, although the clinical diagnosis of osteoblastic meningioma was made.
The patient's presentation and imaging findings are consistent with a metastasis, although the clinical diagnosis of osteoblastic meningioma was made.
The patient's presentation and imaging findings are consistent with a sarcoma, although the clinical diagnosis of osteoblastic meningioma was made.
Histology showed a malignant spindle cell neoplasm, consistent with a malignant tumor.
The patient's presentation and imaging findings are not consistent with a benign tumor, given the malignant histology.
The tumor's extradural location and malignant spindle cell neoplasm characteristics are consistent with Hemangiopericytoma.
